transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I came in because… honestly, it’s getting hard to explain things in a way people can follow. I’m an artist, so I’m used to being a little abstract, and sometimes my work does move between textures and color and meaning, but lately it’s like my thoughts are jumping too fast or too sideways.

Like, I’ll be writing an artist statement and I start with the surface of a piece, the materials, the texture, and then suddenly I’m talking about the budget, or what a client said, or some hidden meaning I feel is connected, and when I read it back it sort of makes sense to me in the moment, but other people say they can’t tell what I’m trying to say. It’s happening in client notes too, not just creative writing, which is embarrassing. And in meetings I’ll be explaining something and people look confused, or they’ll ask me to slow down or repeat myself, and then I realize I’ve skipped three steps and landed somewhere else completely.

So I guess I’m here because it’s starting to affect my work and how I come across. I don’t feel like I’m trying to be confusing, but what comes out doesn’t always line up in a normal order.
Do you find that this jumping between ideas happens to you in most conversations, or is it mainly when you're discussing your art or writing?

It’s… more than just the art now. At first I thought it was only because artist statements are kind of strange anyway, you know, you’re already trying to translate texture and color and meaning into words, so it seemed normal that I’d drift around a bit. But it’s been happening in client notes too, and those are supposed to be straightforward.

Like I’ll start describing a material choice or a surface treatment, and then somehow I’m suddenly talking about the budget, or what the client said last week, or this hidden meaning I feel like is tied to the piece, and I don’t always notice the jump until someone points it out. In meetings it happens out loud too. I’ll think I’m explaining something clearly, but people keep telling me they can’t follow what I’m trying to say, or they ask me to back up because I’ve skipped over the part that connects one idea to the next.

So I guess the answer is it’s not every single conversation, but it’s definitely not only my writing or only when I’m being “artistic.” It’s showing up in regular work conversations too, and that’s what’s been worrying me.
Are you finding that this difficulty with explaining your thoughts is affecting your relationships with clients or colleagues?

Yes. I mean, I wish I could say it was just awkward or that people are being picky, but it’s actually affecting things now.

I’ve missed paid deadlines because I’ll send notes or proposals that I thought were close to finished, and then the client comes back saying they don’t understand what I’m recommending or what the next step is. And then I have to rewrite it, but the rewriting takes longer because I’m trying to make it make sense, and by then the deadline has slipped. It’s embarrassing because these are not just casual ideas in a sketchbook — they’re things people are paying me for.

In meetings, collaborators have gotten visibly confused. Like I’ll be talking about an installation plan, and I think I’m being very clear because in my head all the pieces are connected, but someone will stop me and say, “Wait, are we talking about the materials, the budget, or the layout?” And I realize I’ve somehow braided all of that together without explaining the transitions.

The worst was that an exhibition got postponed because my notes and proposals basically stopped being usable enough. Not completely nonsense, but not solid enough for people to build from or schedule around. That felt really bad, because it wasn’t just me being misunderstood — it actually affected other people’s work and timing.
Are you feeling anxious or self-conscious about speaking with others due to your difficulty explaining your thoughts?

I’m not totally sure how to separate anxiety from just… embarrassment, I guess. I do feel self-conscious sometimes, especially in work settings, because once someone gets that confused look, I can feel myself trying to monitor every sentence while I’m still talking. And then that almost makes it harder, because I’m half explaining and half checking myself from the outside.

But I wouldn’t say I’m scared of people exactly, or that I’m avoiding everyone. It’s more like I get very aware of how I’m coming across. Like, am I making sense, did I skip something, are they being polite but lost, that kind of thing. I’ll sometimes over-explain because I’m trying to prevent the confusion, and then I worry I’ve made it worse by adding too much.

So… yes, self-conscious, definitely. Anxious maybe, but in a situational way, mostly when I know I need to be clear and there are consequences if I’m not.
Have you noticed any changes in your mood, such as feeling more irritable, sad, or euphoric, when you're having trouble explaining your thoughts?

Yeah… I have noticed that, actually. It’s not always in a simple way, like “I’m in a bad mood so I can’t explain myself.” Sometimes it feels almost the opposite at first.

There are stretches where I feel really lit up, like my mind is moving fast but in a good way, and every idea feels connected and important and honestly kind of brilliant. In those moments I feel almost unstoppable, like if people could just keep up with me, they’d see the whole thing the way I do. And when I’m trying to explain something then, I don’t necessarily feel confused inside — I feel like it’s all very clear, almost too clear, but then it comes out in this flood and other people don’t know where I’m going with it.

But then if someone interrupts me or says, “I don’t understand,” or even makes a small comment that I’d normally be able to take fine, I can get irritated really quickly. Like sharper than the situation deserves. A collaborator can ask one practical question, and suddenly I feel like they’re blocking the whole vision or doubting me, and I’ll snap or sound defensive. Then later I’ll think, okay, that reaction was much bigger than what they actually said.

So yes, I think when the explaining gets harder, my mood is often either really elevated, like everything is charged and exciting, or I’m much more irritable than I mean to be.
Do you find yourself getting easily sidetracked by other thoughts or stimuli when you're trying to explain something?

Yes, very much. That’s actually one of the things that makes it so hard to finish anything clearly.

Like if I’m trying to write a proposal, I’ll sit down with a pretty specific intention — explain the concept, outline the materials, make it readable — and then something tiny can pull me completely off course. The buzz of a light above me, or a shadow moving on the wall, or even just seeing one line in an old notebook can suddenly feel like it’s connected to the whole project in some important way. And then instead of writing the proposal, I’m chasing that connection.

It doesn’t always feel like “distraction” in the moment, which is part of the problem. It feels relevant. Like the light buzzing has a rhythm, and then I’m thinking about sound, and then sound becomes part of the installation, and then I’m digging through old notes because I remember one sentence I wrote months ago that suddenly seems essential. By the time I come back, I may have three new ideas, but the actual proposal is still half-written and kind of scattered.

So yes, I get sidetracked easily, but not always by something big. Sometimes it’s really small, almost stupidly small, and then my brain treats it like a doorway into a completely different room.
Do you find it hard to focus on one idea for an extended period when you're trying to explain something?

Yes, I do. It’s hard for me to stay with just one idea long enough to explain it cleanly, especially if I’m writing something like a proposal where I’m supposed to be organized and make a clear case.

I’ll start with one thought, like, okay, I need to describe the concept. But then the buzz of a light, or a shadow on the wall, or even one sentence in an old notebook can pull me completely sideways. And it’s not just that I’m bored or procrastinating, exactly. In the moment it feels like that thing is connected, like it matters, like it’s pointing me toward something I should follow. So I’ll go off into that, and then suddenly I’m not explaining the original idea anymore — I’m in a whole different line of thought.

By the time I come back, if I come back, the original idea feels kind of… interrupted. Like I still know it’s there, but I’ve lost the straight path through it. So yes, focusing on one idea for an extended period is difficult, because almost anything can become a doorway into something else.
Do you often find that your thoughts feel disorganized or fragmented when you're trying to express them to others?

Yes. That’s actually a big part of why I came in, because it’s started showing up in places where I really need to sound clear.

Like with my artist statements, I’ll sit down intending to explain one piece in a normal way — what it’s made of, what I’m trying to explore, maybe the budget or installation needs — and then the statement starts jumping around. I’ll go from talking about textures, like fabric or concrete or the way light hits something, straight into the cost of materials, and then somehow into what I think the piece is secretly pointing to or what a certain pattern “means.” And when I’m writing it, it doesn’t always feel random to me. It feels like there’s a thread connecting all of it. But when I read it back later, or when someone else reads it, it’s like… I can see how they’d be lost.

It happens in client notes too, which is embarrassing. I’ll mean to write something practical, like measurements or changes they asked for, and then I’ll notice I’ve written a whole paragraph about the feeling of the surface or some hidden significance I thought was there, and I didn’t actually answer the basic question.

And in meetings, people keep telling me they can’t follow what I’m trying to explain. I’ll think I’m being thorough, but apparently I’m jumping from one category to another too fast — textures, budget, meaning, logistics, then back to meaning — and I lose them. So yes, fragmented is a good word for it. It’s not that I have no thoughts. It’s more like there are too many pieces, and I can’t always put them in an order other people can understand.
Have you noticed any changes in your overall energy or activity level when you're not trying to explain your thoughts to others?

Yes, definitely. It’s not only when I’m talking or writing that things get kind of… sped up. There are times when my whole activity level just jumps.

Like I’ll suddenly decide I can take on three proposals at once, and it doesn’t feel unreasonable at the time. It feels exciting, like everything is finally moving and I can see all these openings. So I’ll be reorganizing the studio because suddenly the whole layout feels wrong, and then while I’m doing that I’ll start sketching ideas, and then I’ll stay up working on sketches because I don’t want to lose the momentum.

And then it kind of spreads. I’ll be emailing curators, making lists, pulling out materials, cutting pieces for work I haven’t even properly budgeted yet. It’s like I skip the normal order of things. Instead of proposal, budget, materials, schedule, I’m just… doing all of it at once, or starting all of it at once.

At first it can feel productive, honestly. I’ll think, “This is great, I’m finally catching up.” But then I look around and there are half-started projects everywhere, emails sent, the studio torn apart, scraps of material cut for pieces that aren’t actually planned all the way through. So yes, my energy and activity definitely go up sometimes, even when I’m not trying to explain anything to anyone.
Do you experience these difficulties with explaining your thoughts and jumping between ideas all the time, or are there periods where it happens more frequently than others?

It’s not exactly all the time, no. I mean, I can have conversations that are normal enough, especially if it’s something simple or practical. But there are definitely periods where it gets more frequent, and that’s when it becomes obvious to other people.

That’s really why I came in. It started affecting my artist statements, client notes, and meetings in a way I couldn’t just explain away as being “creative” or having a lot of ideas. I’ll be trying to explain a piece and I’ll jump from the texture of the material, to the budget, to some hidden or secret meaning I feel like the work has, and then back to logistics, and it feels connected in my head while I’m saying it or writing it. But then people will look at me like they’re trying to find the main point, and they’ll say they can’t follow what I’m trying to explain.

So it’s not every single minute of every day, but when it’s happening more, it shows up everywhere I have to communicate clearly. It’s like my thoughts don’t stay in lanes. They keep crossing over into each other, and I don’t always notice until someone points it out or I read it back later.
Do you have days or periods where your thoughts feel completely organized and easy to express, without any of the jumping between ideas or confusion?

Yes, there are definitely days where it’s easier. I don’t want to make it sound like every sentence I say is impossible to follow, because that’s not true. If I’m just talking about groceries or a simple schedule thing, or if I’m answering something very direct, I can usually stay with it.

But the reason I came in is because there are enough periods where it doesn’t feel organized at all, especially with my work. My artist statements, client notes, even what I say in meetings — they’ve started jumping around in this way that I can’t always control. I’ll begin with textures, like the feel of a material or how something looks under light, and then suddenly I’m talking about budget, and then I’m explaining some secret meaning I feel like the piece has, and then I’m back to practical details again. In my head, while it’s happening, it feels connected, like I’m following a real line. But other people don’t seem to hear the line.

So, yes, there are clearer days. But when it’s not clear, it’s noticeable enough that people keep telling me they can’t follow what I’m trying to explain, and that’s embarrassing. It makes me second-guess whether I’m actually communicating or just sort of… piling thoughts on top of each other.
Do you consider these difficulties with explaining your thoughts and jumping between ideas to be a constant part of your daily life?

No, I wouldn’t say it’s constant in the sense that every single day, every single conversation is like that. I can still talk plainly about basic things. But it’s been happening enough that it feels like a real pattern, not just one awkward meeting or one messy draft.

What made me come in is that it’s showing up in the places where I really need to be clear — my artist statements, client notes, and even meetings. I’ll start trying to explain a piece by talking about the texture or the surface, then I jump to the budget or materials, then I’m suddenly talking about some secret meaning I feel is inside the work, and then I’m back to practical details again. In my head it feels connected while I’m saying it, but people keep telling me they can’t follow what I’m trying to explain.

So not constant, exactly. More like… when it happens, it spreads into important things, and it makes me worry because I don’t always notice how confusing it sounds until someone reacts to it.
Do you often act on ideas or impulses without fully thinking them through?

Yes, I think I do, especially when I get into one of those “go” modes. It’s not always like I’m doing something obviously reckless on purpose, but I’ll get an idea and I’m already moving before I’ve really checked whether it makes sense.

Like, I’ll suddenly take on three proposals at once because in that moment they all feel possible and exciting, and then I’ll start reorganizing the studio because I’m convinced I need the space to match the new work. Then I’ll be sketching all night, emailing curators, making lists, pulling out materials, and even cutting pieces for work I haven’t budgeted yet. And while I’m doing it, it feels productive, like I’m finally catching the wave of the idea. It doesn’t feel impulsive in the moment — it feels necessary.

But later I’ll look at the emails or the half-started pieces and realize I didn’t really think through the time, the money, or whether I could actually finish all of it. So yes, I guess I do act on ideas before fully thinking them through, especially when I feel very driven by the work.
Are there specific triggers or events that seem to set off these periods where your thoughts feel disorganized and you have trouble explaining them?

I think the biggest trigger is when I have to translate the work into words, if that makes sense. Like, I can be in the studio and the piece itself feels clear to me — the texture, the materials, the color, the way the surface catches light — but then the moment I have to write an artist statement or explain it to a client or talk about it in a meeting, it starts to get tangled.

It’s especially bad when there are practical things mixed in, like budget, deadlines, materials, or what the client wants. I’ll start by describing the texture or the visual idea, and then I’m suddenly talking about cost or logistics, and then I’ll jump into this deeper meaning I feel like the piece has, almost like there’s some hidden message in it, and then I’ll swing back to measurements or invoices or something very practical. In my head it feels like one connected explanation, but I can tell from people’s faces that it’s not landing that way.

So I don’t know if it’s one single event, exactly. It’s more like those situations where I’m expected to explain my art clearly — statements, client notes, meetings — seem to set it off or at least make it really obvious. That’s when people keep saying they can’t follow me, and that’s what made me feel like I needed to come in.
Are there times when you feel completely in control of your thoughts and can express yourself clearly without any difficulty?

Yes, there are definitely times when I can be clear. I don’t want to make it sound like every time I open my mouth everything comes out scrambled, because that’s not true. If I’m talking about something simple, or if I’m just working quietly and not having to explain it, I can usually say what I mean.

But the problem is that in the situations that matter most for my work, it doesn’t always stay that way. I came in because my artist statements, client notes, and even things I say in meetings have started jumping around — like I’ll begin with the textures or the surface of a piece, then suddenly I’m talking about budgets or materials, and then I’ll drift into what feels like the secret meaning inside it, and then back to logistics again. In my head it feels like I’m explaining one whole connected thing, but people keep telling me they can’t follow what I’m trying to say.

So yes, I do have clear moments. It’s just that I can’t always count on them when I need them. And that’s what scares me a little, because professionally I need to be able to translate the work into words.
Are your difficulties with explaining your thoughts and jumping between ideas causing problems in your personal relationships outside of work?

It’s… I think it’s mostly showing up around work, honestly. That’s where people are really telling me they can’t follow me — like with artist statements, client notes, meetings, when I’m trying to explain a piece and I start with the texture or the surface, then I’m suddenly talking about budgets, then somehow I’m talking about what feels like the hidden or secret meaning of it, and then I’m back to materials or timelines. In my head it still feels connected, but I can see that other people don’t experience it that way.

Outside of work, with personal relationships, it’s harder for me to say. I don’t think it’s causing the same kind of obvious problem, because my friends aren’t asking me to make a proposal or explain a commission. But I do think sometimes people close to me get impatient or kind of quiet when I’m talking, like they’re waiting for me to land the plane. So maybe it does affect them a little, but the place where it’s become a real problem — the reason I came in — is the professional stuff, because I need people to understand what I’m explaining.
Are you experiencing any difficulties in your personal relationships due to the way you express your thoughts?

A little, maybe, but it’s not as obvious there as it is with work. With friends or family, they’re not usually asking me to explain a whole concept or justify a piece, so it doesn’t get exposed in the same way.

The main reason I came in is really because of the professional side — my artist statements, client notes, and even things I say in meetings have started to jump around. I’ll be trying to explain a piece and I start with the texture or the surface, then suddenly I’m talking about the budget, then I’m on this whole other track about what feels like the secret meaning of it, and then I’m back to materials or timelines. In my head it all feels connected, but other people keep telling me they can’t follow what I’m trying to explain.

In personal relationships, I think people sometimes get quiet or look a little lost, but they’re more forgiving, I guess. It’s causing the biggest problems when I need to be understood clearly.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others or blurting out answers before they finish speaking?

I’m not sure I’d say I often do that. I mean, I probably interrupt sometimes, like anyone does, especially if I’m worried I’ll lose what I was about to say, but I haven’t really noticed it as a major pattern where I’m constantly cutting people off or blurting answers before they finish.

It’s more like… if I’m already trying to hold a thought in my head, I might jump in too soon because I’m afraid the thread will disappear. But I don’t know if other people would describe me as someone who interrupts a lot. No one has really come to me and said, “You keep talking over me,” at least not in a way that stands out.

So I guess my answer is: not especially, or not that I’m aware of. If it happens, it’s probably occasional rather than something I recognize as a big problem.
Do you often feel restless or fidgety when you're sitting still or engaging in quiet activities?

I don’t think so, not in a way that I’d call a major issue. I mean, I can get physically uncomfortable if I’ve been sitting for a long time, like anyone, and sometimes I’ll shift around or change positions, especially if I’m in a chair that feels awkward or if I’m trying to concentrate.

But do I feel like I’m constantly restless or like I can’t sit still during quiet things? I don’t really know that I experience it that way. If I’m doing something quiet, like looking at images, sketching, reading something short, or just sitting with coffee, I’m usually able to stay there. I might play with a pen or touch the edge of paper or move my foot without thinking, but I haven’t noticed it as this overwhelming urge to get up and move around.

So I guess my answer is… not especially. Maybe a little normal fidgeting, but not something that stands out to me as a real problem.
Do you often have difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities?

Yes, I think that one is actually more of a problem for me. It’s not that I can’t ever focus, because I can, especially if I’m really absorbed in something visual or hands-on. But when I’m trying to do something that needs a straight line of attention, like writing a proposal or putting together a description for a project, I get pulled off so easily.

It can be something really small, like the buzz of a light in the room, or a shadow moving on the wall, or I’ll notice one line in an old notebook sitting nearby, and suddenly I’m not writing the proposal anymore. I’m following that line into some completely different idea, or I’m looking up something related to it, or I’m sketching something that feels urgent for a minute. In my mind it doesn’t always feel like I’m “distracted” at first — it feels connected, like, “Oh, this matters too” — but then I look up and realize I’ve drifted pretty far from what I was supposed to be doing.

So, yes, sustaining attention can be hard, especially with writing or planning tasks where I have to keep returning to the main point.

There are stretches where I feel really lit up, like my mind is moving fast but in a good way, and every idea feels connected and important and honestly kind of brilliant. In those moments I feel almost unstoppable, like if people could just keep up with me, they’d see the whole thing the way I do. And when I’m trying to explain something then, I don’t necessarily feel confused inside — I feel like it’s all very clear, almost too clear, but then it comes out in this flood and other people don’t know where I’m going with it.

But then if someone interrupts me or says, “I don’t understand,” or even makes a small comment that I’d normally be able to take fine, I can get irritated really quickly. Like sharper than the situation deserves. A collaborator can ask one practical question, and suddenly I feel like they’re blocking the whole vision or doubting me, and I’ll snap or sound defensive. Then later I’ll think, okay, that reaction was much bigger than what they actually said.

So yes, I think when the explaining gets harder, my mood is often either really elevated, like everything is charged and exciting, or I’m much more irritable than I mean to be.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's difficulty with explaining thoughts is associated with distractibility
doctor.question: Do you find yourself getting easily sidetracked by other thoughts or stimuli when you're trying to explain something?

target_item.name: Manic_Distractibility
target_item.manifestation: When I try to write a proposal, the buzz of a light, a shadow on the wall, or one line in an old notebook can pull me off task and send me into something completely different.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about being easily sidetracked by other thoughts or external stimuli while trying to explain something, which most directly matches distractibility.

patient.answer:
Yes, very much. That’s actually one of the things that makes it so hard to finish anything clearly.

Like if I’m trying to write a proposal, I’ll sit down with a pretty specific intention — explain the concept, outline the materials, make it readable — and then something tiny can pull me completely off course. The buzz of a light above me, or a shadow moving on the wall, or even just seeing one line in an old notebook can suddenly feel like it’s connected to the whole project in some important way. And then instead of writing the proposal, I’m chasing that connection.

It doesn’t always feel like “distraction” in the moment, which is part of the problem. It feels relevant. Like the light buzzing has a rhythm, and then I’m thinking about sound, and then sound becomes part of the installation, and then I’m digging through old notes because I remember one sentence I wrote months ago that suddenly seems essential. By the time I come back, I may have three new ideas, but the actual proposal is still half-written and kind of scattered.

So yes, I get sidetracked easily, but not always by something big. Sometimes it’s really small, almost stupidly small, and then my brain treats it like a doorway into a completely different room.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's difficulty with explaining thoughts is associated with a lack of focus or attention
doctor.question: Do you find it hard to focus on one idea for an extended period when you're trying to explain something?

target_item.name: Manic_Distractibility
target_item.manifestation: When I try to write a proposal, the buzz of a light, a shadow on the wall, or one line in an old notebook can pull me off task and send me into something completely different.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty sustaining focus on one idea while explaining, which most directly relates to distractibility and being pulled off task.

patient.answer:
Yes, I do. It’s hard for me to stay with just one idea long enough to explain it cleanly, especially if I’m writing something like a proposal where I’m supposed to be organized and make a clear case.

I’ll start with one thought, like, okay, I need to describe the concept. But then the buzz of a light, or a shadow on the wall, or even one sentence in an old notebook can pull me completely sideways. And it’s not just that I’m bored or procrastinating, exactly. In the moment it feels like that thing is connected, like it matters, like it’s pointing me toward something I should follow. So I’ll go off into that, and then suddenly I’m not explaining the original idea anymore — I’m in a whole different line of thought.

By the time I come back, if I come back, the original idea feels kind of… interrupted. Like I still know it’s there, but I’ve lost the straight path through it. So yes, focusing on one idea for an extended period is difficult, because almost anything can become a doorway into something else.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's difficulty with explaining thoughts is associated with disorganized thinking patterns
doctor.question: Do you often find that your thoughts feel disorganized or fragmented when you're trying to express them to others?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Thinking_Speech
target_item.manifestation: I came in because my artist statements, client notes, and even what I say in meetings have started jumping from textures to budgets to secret meanings, and people keep telling me they can’t follow what I’m trying to explain.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether thoughts feel disorganized or fragmented when expressing them to others, which matches disorganized thinking and speech.

patient.answer:
Yes. That’s actually a big part of why I came in, because it’s started showing up in places where I really need to sound clear.

Like with my artist statements, I’ll sit down intending to explain one piece in a normal way — what it’s made of, what I’m trying to explore, maybe the budget or installation needs — and then the statement starts jumping around. I’ll go from talking about textures, like fabric or concrete or the way light hits something, straight into the cost of materials, and then somehow into what I think the piece is secretly pointing to or what a certain pattern “means.” And when I’m writing it, it doesn’t always feel random to me. It feels like there’s a thread connecting all of it. But when I read it back later, or when someone else reads it, it’s like… I can see how they’d be lost.

It happens in client notes too, which is embarrassing. I’ll mean to write something practical, like measurements or changes they asked for, and then I’ll notice I’ve written a whole paragraph about the feeling of the surface or some hidden significance I thought was there, and I didn’t actually answer the basic question.

And in meetings, people keep telling me they can’t follow what I’m trying to explain. I’ll think I’m being thorough, but apparently I’m jumping from one category to another too fast — textures, budget, meaning, logistics, then back to meaning — and I lose them. So yes, fragmented is a good word for it. It’s not that I have no thoughts. It’s more like there are too many pieces, and I can’t always put them in an order other people can understand.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's difficulty with explaining thoughts is associated with a significant change in their overall activity level
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your overall energy or activity level when you're not trying to explain your thoughts to others?

target_item.name: Increased_Activity

patient.answer:
Yes, definitely. It’s not only when I’m talking or writing that things get kind of… sped up. There are times when my whole activity level just jumps.

Like I’ll suddenly decide I can take on three proposals at once, and it doesn’t feel unreasonable at the time. It feels exciting, like everything is finally moving and I can see all these openings. So I’ll be reorganizing the studio because suddenly the whole layout feels wrong, and then while I’m doing that I’ll start sketching ideas, and then I’ll stay up working on sketches because I don’t want to lose the momentum.

And then it kind of spreads. I’ll be emailing curators, making lists, pulling out materials, cutting pieces for work I haven’t even properly budgeted yet. It’s like I skip the normal order of things. Instead of proposal, budget, materials, schedule, I’m just… doing all of it at once, or starting all of it at once.

At first it can feel productive, honestly. I’ll think, “This is great, I’m finally catching up.” But then I look around and there are half-started projects everywhere, emails sent, the studio torn apart, scraps of material cut for pieces that aren’t actually planned all the way through. So yes, my energy and activity definitely go up sometimes, even when I’m not trying to explain anything to anyone.

It’s not exactly all the time, no. I mean, I can have conversations that are normal enough, especially if it’s something simple or practical. But there are definitely periods where it gets more frequent, and that’s when it becomes obvious to other people.

That’s really why I came in. It started affecting my artist statements, client notes, and meetings in a way I couldn’t just explain away as being “creative” or having a lot of ideas. I’ll be trying to explain a piece and I’ll jump from the texture of the material, to the budget, to some hidden or secret meaning I feel like the work has, and then back to logistics, and it feels connected in my head while I’m saying it or writing it. But then people will look at me like they’re trying to find the main point, and they’ll say they can’t follow what I’m trying to explain.

So it’s not every single minute of every day, but when it’s happening more, it shows up everywhere I have to communicate clearly. It’s like my thoughts don’t stay in lanes. They keep crossing over into each other, and I don’t always notice until someone points it out or I read it back later.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's difficulties with explaining thoughts are persistent or episodic

patient.answer:
Yes, there are definitely days where it’s easier. I don’t want to make it sound like every sentence I say is impossible to follow, because that’s not true. If I’m just talking about groceries or a simple schedule thing, or if I’m answering something very direct, I can usually stay with it.

But the reason I came in is because there are enough periods where it doesn’t feel organized at all, especially with my work. My artist statements, client notes, even what I say in meetings — they’ve started jumping around in this way that I can’t always control. I’ll begin with textures, like the feel of a material or how something looks under light, and then suddenly I’m talking about budget, and then I’m explaining some secret meaning I feel like the piece has, and then I’m back to practical details again. In my head, while it’s happening, it feels connected, like I’m following a real line. But other people don’t seem to hear the line.

So, yes, there are clearer days. But when it’s not clear, it’s noticeable enough that people keep telling me they can’t follow what I’m trying to explain, and that’s embarrassing. It makes me second-guess whether I’m actually communicating or just sort of… piling thoughts on top of each other.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are persistent or episodic
doctor.question: Are there specific triggers or events that seem to set off these periods where your thoughts feel disorganized and you have trouble explaining them?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Thinking_Speech
target_item.manifestation: I came in because my artist statements, client notes, and even what I say in meetings have started jumping from textures to budgets to secret meanings, and people keep telling me they can’t follow what I’m trying to explain.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about triggers for periods when thoughts feel disorganized and explanations become hard to follow, which directly concerns disorganized thinking and speech.

patient.answer:
I think the biggest trigger is when I have to translate the work into words, if that makes sense. Like, I can be in the studio and the piece itself feels clear to me — the texture, the materials, the color, the way the surface catches light — but then the moment I have to write an artist statement or explain it to a client or talk about it in a meeting, it starts to get tangled.

It’s especially bad when there are practical things mixed in, like budget, deadlines, materials, or what the client wants. I’ll start by describing the texture or the visual idea, and then I’m suddenly talking about cost or logistics, and then I’ll jump into this deeper meaning I feel like the piece has, almost like there’s some hidden message in it, and then I’ll swing back to measurements or invoices or something very practical. In my head it feels like one connected explanation, but I can tell from people’s faces that it’s not landing that way.

So I don’t know if it’s one single event, exactly. It’s more like those situations where I’m expected to explain my art clearly — statements, client notes, meetings — seem to set it off or at least make it really obvious. That’s when people keep saying they can’t follow me, and that’s what made me feel like I needed to come in.

So yes, I do have clear moments. It’s just that I can’t always count on them when I need them. And that’s what scares me a little, because professionally I need to be able to translate the work into words.
